subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
The accountant of Moon Limited provides you the following information: (i) Provision for doubtful debts was created @3% till 31st March, 2025; from FY 2025-26, the rate has been changed to 5%. (ii) During the year ended 31st March, 2026 the management has introduced a formal gratuity scheme in place of ad-hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement. (iii) During 2025-26, there was change in cost formula in measuring the cost of inventories. (iv) Management decided to pay pension to employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service (₹25,000 per month); earlier there was no such pension scheme.

You are required to advise the accountant of Moon Limited, with valid reasons, whether the above transactions would be treated as change in accounting policy or not, for the year ended 31st March, 2026 in the context of AS 5. (4 Marks)
answer_html:
As per para 21 of AS 5, the preparation of financial statements involves making estimates based on circumstances existing when the statements are prepared; it may be necessary to revise an estimate in a subsequent period if circumstances change. Revision of an estimate, by its nature, does not bring the adjustment within the definitions of a prior period item or an extraordinary item. Change in Accounting estimate is not a change in accounting policy.

(i) Provision for doubtful debts rate change (3% to 5%): this is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy. Per para 27 of AS 5, a change in estimate with a material effect in the current period should be disclosed and quantified; any change expected to have a material effect in later periods should also be disclosed and quantified.

(ii) As per AS 5, adopting an accounting policy for events or transactions that differ in substance from previously occurring events or transactions is not considered a change in accounting policy. Accordingly, introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments is not a change in accounting policy.

(iii) As per AS 2 and AS 5: the method of determining cost (FIFO/Weighted Average) is an accounting policy choice, and any change in it affects measurement of inventory and profit. Hence a change in cost formula in measuring the cost of inventories IS a change in Accounting Policy.

(iv) The adoption of a new accounting policy for events or transactions which did not occur previously, or that were immaterial, will not be treated as a change in accounting policy. Introducing a pension scheme where none previously existed is therefore not a change in accounting policy.

topics.title: Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies
topics.label: AS 5 (2.5)

examiner_comment.text: Many examinees classified the provision-rate change and the new gratuity/pension schemes as changes in accounting policy, not recognising AS 5's distinction between a genuine policy change (like the inventory cost-formula change) and a change in estimate or the adoption of a policy for a genuinely new type of transaction.

answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹3,30,000 — only the portion of interest attributable to the loan-funded (not grant-funded) part of the qualifying-asset spend is capitalised (loan-funded: building 30 + machinery 20 = 50 out of the total 50 lakh loan, i.e. the entire loan is loan-funded qualifying spend); apportioned against total interest of ₹5,50,000 for the fraction of the year/qualifying use, per AS 16.

(ii) It is not distributable as a dividend. (iii) It is treated as a capital reserve. (iv) It is not distributable as a dividend but considered as deferred income.

KPK Limited is installing a new Plant: Cost per supplier's invoice ₹45,00,000; Estimated dismantling costs after 5 years ₹3,25,000; Initial operating losses before commercial production ₹4,00,000; Interest paid to supplier for deferred credit ₹2,50,000; Initial delivery and handling costs ₹1,85,000; Cost of site preparation ₹5,00,000; Consultants' fees for acquisition advice ₹6,75,000.   2. 14500 Shares
  3. Nil Shares

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: SR Limited manufactures finished goods 'MP' from raw material 'RP'. Year ended 31st March 2025: Opening Inventory MP 4,000 units ₹1,20,000; RP 4,400 units ₹52,800. Purchase of RP 40,000 units ₹4,80,000. Labour ₹3,23,200. Fixed Overheads ₹3,15,000. Sales 40,200 units ₹11,20,000. Closing Inventory: MP 4,200 units; RP 4,000 units. Expected production 45,000 units of MP. Due to fall in market demand, sales price of MP fell to ₹22/unit; replacement cost of RP ₹11.50/unit on closing day. Calculate the value of Closing Stock of 'MP' and 'RP' as on 31st March 2025.
answer_html:
W.N.1 Actual production: Sales 40,200 + Closing FG 4,200 − Opening FG 4,000 = 40,400 units.

W.N.2 RP consumed: Opening RP 4,400 + Purchases 40,000 = 44,400 available; less Closing RP 4,000 = 40,400 units consumed (1 unit RP per unit MP produced).

W.N.3 Cost per unit RP (weighted average): (Opening value 52,800 + Purchases 4,80,000) / 44,400 units = 5,32,800/44,400 = ₹12.00/unit.

Cost of Material Consumed (40,400 × ₹12)4,84,800
Direct Labour3,23,200
Fixed Overhead (3,15,000 × 40,400/45,000 — based on normal/expected production, not actual)2,82,800
Cost of Production10,90,800
Cost per unit (10,90,800/40,400)₹27
Net Realisable Value per unit (selling price)₹22

Since NRV (₹22) is less than cost (₹27), the closing MP inventory is valued at NRV. Since finished goods NRV is below cost, the raw material RP feeding it is valued at replacement cost (₹11.50), per AS 2's write-down rule.

Value of closing inventory: MP (4,200 × ₹22) = ₹92,400. RP (4,000 × ₹11.50) = ₹46,000.

examiner_comment.text: The performance of examinees in this part was not satisfactory. A majority of them were unable to determine the value of closing inventory of finished goods (MP) and raw materials (RP) in accordance with AS 2 "Valuation of Inventories". Several examinees failed to compute the cost of production correctly, particularly where certain items required proportionate allocation. Many could ascertain only the labour cost of ₹3,23,200, while the remaining elements of cost were incorrectly computed. Further, a large number of examinees valued the closing stock of finished goods (on NRV basis) and raw materials (on replacement cost basis) incorrectly.

question_html: XY Limited recognized dividend income of ₹10 lakhs on accrual basis on securities of face value ₹100 lakhs held at 31st March 2025. The dividend (10%) was declared on 30th April 2025, having been proposed on 30th March 2025. Comment.

question_html: XY Limited sold goods of ₹1,50,000 on approval basis on 15th December 2024; approval period 3 months, after which goods are considered sold. answer_html: Incorrect as recognised. For goods sold on approval, revenue should not be recognised until formal acceptance, an act adopting the transaction, or expiry of the rejection period. Revenue for ₹90,000 (60%) should be recognised on 31st January, 2025 (date of approval); the remaining ₹60,000 should be recognised on 15th March, 2025, when the 3-month approval period lapsed without response (deemed acceptance) — not the full ₹1,50,000 on 15th December, 2024 as the accountant did.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Grace Limited acquired the business (a cash-generating unit) of Venus Limited on 31st March 2023 for ₹8,000 lakhs: Fair value of identifiable assets ₹6,000 lakhs, Goodwill (amortised over 5 years) ₹2,000 lakhs. Anticipated useful life of acquired assets: 8 years, nil residual value, straight-line. On 31st March 2025, significant decline in production estimated due to government policy changes; net selling price of identifiable assets ₹3,000 lakhs. Cash flow forecast for next 6 years (₹ lakhs): 1,000/800/700/800/600/500. Discount rate 10% (PV factors: 0.909, 0.826, 0.751, 0.683, 0.621, 0.564). Calculate: (i) Value in use at 31 March 2025; (ii) Impairment loss for year ended 31 March 2025; (iii) Revised carrying amount of asset.
answer_html:
(i) Value in Use: 1,000×0.909=909.00 + 800×0.826=660.80 + 700×0.751=525.70 + 800×0.683=546.40 + 600×0.621=372.60 + 500×0.564=282.00 = ₹3,296.50 lakhs, rounded to ₹3,297 lakhs.

Carrying amount at 31.3.2025 (2 years post-acquisition): Goodwill 2,000 − amortisation (2,000/5×2=800) = 1,200. Identifiable assets 6,000 − depreciation (6,000/8×2=1,500) = 4,500. Total CGU carrying amount = 5,700.

Recoverable amount = higher of Value in Use (3,297) and net selling price of identifiable assets (3,000, no CGU-wide fair-value-less-costs-to-sell given) = 3,297 (since 3,297 > 3,000).

(ii) Impairment loss = Carrying amount (5,700) − Recoverable amount (3,297) = ₹2,403 lakhs.

(iii) Allocation: per AS 28, impairment is allocated first to goodwill (written down to zero: full 1,200 absorbed), then the remainder (2,403−1,200=1,203) to identifiable assets pro-rata: revised carrying amount of identifiable asset = 4,500−1,203 = ₹3,297 lakhs (goodwill: Nil).

examiner_comment.text: A majority of examinees were unable to compute the impairment loss and allocate the same appropriately among the assets of the CGU as per the requirements of AS 28 "Impairment of Assets". Many examinees failed to determine the value in use, impairment loss and the revised carrying amount of assets, evidencing an inadequate understanding of the impairment principles.

question_html: Seva Limited and subsidiary Meva Limited, Balance Sheets as at 31st March 2025 (₹ Lakh): Seva — Equity Shares of ₹10 6,000, General Reserve 1,500, P&L 2,000, 10% Debentures 1,180, Trade Payable 1,500; Land and Building 4,000, Plant & Machinery 1,460, Investments (Meva shares) 3,000, Inventories 1,400, Trade Receivable 1,420, Cash at Bank 550, Cash in Hand 350. Meva — Equity Shares of ₹10 4,000, General Reserve 1,200, P&L 1,500, 10% Debentures 820, Trade Payable 1,080; Land and Building 4,150, Plant & Machinery 1,650, Inventories 1,100, Trade Receivable 1,000, Cash at Bank 600, Cash in Hand 100. Seva acquired 80% of Meva on 1st April 2024 (Meva's General Reserve ₹2,000 lakh, P&L ₹800 lakh on that date). On 1st November 2024, Meva issued a 1:3 bonus share out of General Reserve (as at 31 March 2024 balance). On 31st March 2025, Seva's inventory includes goods purchased from Meva for ₹125 lakh, on which Meva made a profit of ₹25 lakh. Prepare the Consolidated Balance Sheet as per Schedule III.
answer_html:
W.N.9 Bonus shares: Meva's shares post-bonus 4,000 lakh (at ₹10 face value, i.e. 400 lakh shares) represent 4/3 of pre-bonus holding; pre-bonus = 4,000×3/4=3,000; bonus issued = 4,000−3,000=1,000 (lakh, i.e. ₹1,000 lakh face value), funded from General Reserve.

W.N.1 Meva's General Reserve movement: Opening 2,000 − Bonus 1,000 + transfer from P&L 200 = Closing 1,200.

W.N.2 Meva's P&L movement: Opening 800 − transfer to General Reserve 200 + Net profit for the year (balancing) 900 = Closing 1,500.

W.N.4 Capital profits (pre-acquisition): General Reserve at acquisition, net of the bonus issue (2,000−1,000=1,000) + P&L at acquisition (800) = 1,800. Seva's 80% share = 1,440; Minority's 20% = 360.

W.N.3 Revenue profits (post-acquisition): 900 (from W.N.2); Seva's 80% share: General Reserve 160 (80% of 200) + P&L 560 (80% of 700, i.e. profit after removing the amount already transferred to reserve) = 720; Minority's 20% = 180.

W.N.5 Capital Reserve: Paid-up value of shares held (80% of 4,000) 3,200 + share in capital profits 1,440 = 4,640; less cost of shares 3,000 = Capital Reserve ₹1,640 lakh.

W.N.6 Minority Interest: 20% of share capital (800) + share in revenue profits (180) + share in capital profits (360) = 1,340; less unrealised profit (20% of 25 = 5, Meva's share of the inter-company profit since Meva is the seller) = Minority Interest ₹1,335 lakh.

Consolidated Balance Sheet as at 31st March, 2025 (₹ Lakh): Share Capital 6,000 (Seva's own, unchanged); Reserves and Surplus 5,840 (Capital Reserve 1,640 + General Reserve 1,660 + P&L 2,540); Minority Interest 1,335; Long-term borrowings 2,000 (1,180+820); Trade payables 2,580 (1,500+1,080). Total 17,755. Assets: PPE 11,260 (Land&Building 8,150 [4,000+4,150] + Plant&Machinery 3,110 [1,460+1,650]); Inventories 2,475 (1,400+1,100−25 unrealised profit); Trade receivables 2,420 (1,420+1,000); Cash and cash equivalents 1,600 (Bank 1,150 + Cash in hand 450). Total 17,755.

Several examinees failed to give the correct treatment to the issue of bonus shares and the unrealised profit included in closing inventory arising from an upstream transaction. subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Sneha, an employee of Omre Limited, went on paid maternity leave for 9 months, 1st January 2024 to 30th September 2024, monthly pay ₹1,50,000. While preparing FY2023-24 financial statements, her salary for 3 months (Jan–Mar 2024) was omitted. When she joined 1st October 2024, the whole 9-month salary was paid. With reference to AS-5, determine if this is a prior period item and pass the FY2024-25 journal entry. Variant: Suppose Sneha was terminated 1st January 2024 and reinstated by court order on 30th September 2024, with the 9-month salary paid 1st October 2024 — what is the AS-5 treatment here, with journal entry?
answer_html:
Original scenario: Per AS 5, prior period items are income/expenses arising in the current period from errors or omissions in preparing prior periods' financial statements. The 3 months' salary (Jan–Mar 2024, ₹4,50,000) omitted from FY2023-24 is a prior period item in FY2024-25.

Journal entry (FY2024-25): Salary A/c (₹1,50,000×6) Dr. 9,00,000; Prior Period Item A/c (₹1,50,000×3) Dr. 4,50,000; To Bank A/c 13,50,000.

Variant (termination/reinstatement): AS 5 states "prior period items" does not include adjustments necessitated by circumstances that, though related to prior periods, are determined only in the current period. Since Sneha's reinstatement (with retrospective salary) was ordered by the court only in FY2024-25, the ₹4,50,000 (Jan–Mar 2024) is not a prior period item — the entire ₹13,50,000 is a current-year expense.

Journal entry (variant): Salary A/c (₹1,50,000×9) Dr. 13,50,000; To Bank A/c 13,50,000.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: What are the key elements of financial statements? Explain.
answer_html:
1. Assets: a resource controlled by the enterprise from past events, expected to bring future economic benefits (e.g. plant, patents, receivables).
  2. Liabilities: a present obligation arising from past events, settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits (e.g. borrowings, provisions).
  3. Equity: the residual interest in assets after deducting all liabilities — owners' claim (capital, reserves), distinct from liabilities (claims of parties other than owners); changes through contributions/distributions or income/expenses.
  4. Income/Gain: increases in economic benefits through inflow of assets or reduction of liabilities, increasing equity (includes revenue and gains).
  5. Expenses/Loss: decreases in economic benefits through outflows/depletion of assets or incurrence of liabilities, decreasing equity (other than distributions to owners) — expenses arise in the ordinary course (e.g. wages); losses may or may not (e.g. loss on PPE disposal), and are shown separately to aid performance assessment.

case_facts_html:

During the year 5, the Company has completed 1 stretch of 100 kms which is operational between two points and is capable of intended use.

Based on the information given above, answer Question No. 1 (a)–(d).

  4. ₹60 Lakhs
answer_html: Answer: (iii) ₹63 Lakhs = ₹70 Lakhs interest − ₹7 Lakhs temporary-investment income (net borrowing cost eligible for capitalisation while surplus funds are invested pending use).

subject: Advanced Accounting
case_facts_html:
Gases Ltd. is installing a 2,000 kms long gas pipeline for distribution of gasses (Project is a qualifying asset as per AS 16). For this purpose it borrowed funds for ₹700 Lakhs at subsidised rates and has to pay annually an interest of ₹70 Lakhs. The Company has also invested unused funds and is earning an income of ₹7 Lakhs annually. During the next year the Company used all funds and no income is now being earned. During the year 5, the Company has completed 1 stretch of 100 kms which is operational between two points and is capable of intended use.

Based on the information given above, answer Question No. 1 (a)–(d).
question_html:
For the year 5, how much borrowing cost should be expensed:

  1. ₹7 Lakhs
  2. ₹6 Lakhs
  3. ₹3.5 Lakhs
  4. Nil
answer_html: Answer: (iii) ₹3.5 Lakhs — the completed 100 km stretch is 5% of the 2,000 km pipeline; capitalisation ceases for that part (5% × ₹70 Lakhs) while the rest of the project continues under construction.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees expensed the full year-5 interest or none at all, not applying the proportionate cessation rule for the completed 5%-of-total-length stretch that is separately capable of use.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html:
A dealer in machinery, Shakti Equipments Pvt. Ltd., leased out one of its machines to Delta Tools Ltd. on a 3-year operating lease, with equal annual lease rentals intended to yield a 20% profit margin on the cost of the machinery (₹3,00,000). Economic life of the machinery is 5 years; total expected output over its useful life: Year I 50,000 units, Year II 60,000, Year III 40,000, Year IV 65,000, Year V 85,000. Delta Tools will use the machine for Years I–III only, then return it. Compute the annual lease rent that provides the dealer a 20% profit margin on cost.

  1. ₹30,000
  2. ₹60,000
  3. ₹50,000
  4. ₹36,000
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000. Total amount the dealer targets recovering over the machine's full economic life = cost + 20% margin = ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000. Since this is an operating lease, the dealer recovers this target progressively, in proportion to how much of the machine's total lifetime output/value is consumed during each period of use — not by amortising the full amount over just the 3-year lease term. Output during the 3-year lease (Years I–III): 50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units, exactly 50% of the machine's total 5-year output (3,00,000 units). The dealer therefore targets recovering 50% of ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000 during this lease, as equal annual rentals over the 3 years: ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000/year.

examiner_comment.text: A common error is spreading the full cost-plus-margin total evenly over only the 3-year lease term (giving ₹1,20,000/year, not a listed option), missing that the dealer only needs to recover the portion of value corresponding to the output consumed during this particular lease, since the machine still has 2 years/half its output-value left when it is returned.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: A private limited company manufacturing fancy terry towels had valued its closing inventory of finished goods at realisable value, inclusive of profit and export cash incentives. Firm contracts had been received and goods were packed for export, but ownership had not been transferred to the foreign buyers. Comment on the valuation of the inventories by the company.
answer_html:
AS 2 requires inventories to be valued at the lower of historical cost and net realisable value. AS 9 permits valuing goods at net realisable value only in specific industries where performance is substantially complete prior to the transaction generating revenue — e.g. harvested agricultural crops or extracted mineral ores, where a sale is assured under forward contract/government guarantee or a ready market exists with negligible risk of failure to sell.

Fancy terry towels do not fall into the agricultural-crop or mineral-ore category. Since ownership had not transferred to the foreign buyers, the sale was not yet complete. The closing inventory should therefore have been valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, not at net realisable value. Further, export cash incentives are recognised only in the year the export sale actually takes place, not accrued into inventory valuation ahead of the sale. The company's valuation policy is therefore not correct.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees accepted the NRV-inclusive-of-profit valuation on the basis of firm export contracts alone, not recognising that the AS 9 exception is limited to specific industries (agricultural/mineral) and does not extend to manufactured goods merely because a sale contract exists.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd., preparing FY2024-25 financial statements. After year-end: (a) Fire on 10th April, 2025 destroyed uninsured stock worth ₹10,00,000, salvage recovered ₹2,00,000. (b) Legal claim filed 18th April, 2025 alleging misleading advertisement, damages claimed ₹20,00,000. (c) Cheques in Hand: company proposes recognising all cheques dated 31st March, 2025 or earlier received from stockists as "Cheques in Hand" under Cash and Cash Equivalents, reducing Trade Receivables — but two categories exist: (i) cheques physically collected by marketing personnel on/before 31st March, 2025; (ii) cheques sent by courier on/before 31st March but received only in April 2025. All cheques were deposited and realized in April 2025. Comment on the accounting treatment for each.
answer_html:
(a) Fire and loss of uninsured stock: occurred after the balance sheet date and does not relate to any condition existing on 31st March, 2025 — a non-adjusting event. Given its materiality (uninsured stock, future risk exposure), the fire and uninsured position must be disclosed, including its nature, estimated financial effect, and future vulnerability if determinable.

(b) Legal suit: initiated after the balance sheet date, no additional evidence of a pre-existing condition — also non-adjusting. Per AS 4 para 16, disclose as a contingent liability, including the nature of the contingency, estimated financial effect, and outcome uncertainties.

(c)(i) Cheques collected by marketing personnel: physically collected on or before 31st March, 2025 — since marketing personnel act as company representatives, this constitutes receipt by the company itself, discharging the stockist's liability. This is an adjusting event: reduce Trade Receivables and recognise as Cheques in Hand under Cash and Cash Equivalents, with appropriate accounting-policy disclosure.

(c)(ii) Cheques sent by courier, received only in April: though dated on/before 31st March, they were not in the company's possession until after the balance sheet date — a non-adjusting event. Account for these in the period actually received (April 2025), regardless of the cheque date; no disclosure needed since the event does not materially affect the financial position.

topics.title: Contingencies and Events occurring after the Balance Sheet Date
topics.label: AS 4 (1.5)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees treated all cheques dated on or before 31st March as adjusting events based on the cheque date alone, missing that physical possession by the company (or its representative) by the balance sheet date, not the cheque's date, is what actually determines adjusting vs. non-adjusting treatment.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Identify each of the following as Change in Accounting Policy / Change in Accounting Estimate / Extraordinary Item / Prior Period Item / Ordinary Activity: (i) Non-provision for salary already due in an earlier year. (ii) Attachment of the property of the enterprise. (iii) Introduction of a new pension scheme for employees. (iv) Change in Reserve for obsolete inventory. (v) Settlement of a litigation case. (vi) Legislative changes with long-term retrospective application. (vii) Change from Cost Model to Revaluation Model for PPE measurement. (viii) Government-sanctioned grant received this year for expenses incurred in a previous year.
answer_html:
1. Prior period item.
  2. Extraordinary item.
  3. Ordinary activity (not a change in accounting policy).
  4. Change in accounting estimate.
  5. Ordinary activity, but requires separate disclosure.
  6. Extraordinary item requiring separate disclosure.
  7. Change in accounting policy.
  8. Prior period item.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Best Ltd., a consultancy services provider, received a GST department demand notice of ₹2,50,000 on consultancy services provided; the company paid the demand and recorded it as extraordinary expenditure. Can this payment of a tax demand be recognised as an extraordinary item?
answer_html: No. Per AS 5, extraordinary items arise from events clearly distinct from ordinary activities and are not expected to recur frequently or regularly. Providing consultancy services is Best Ltd.'s ordinary business activity, and the GST liability arises directly from these ordinary transactions. Paying a tax demand raised by the taxation authority is part of normal business operations. Recording it as extraordinary is therefore not correct — it should be recognised as part of profit or loss from ordinary activities.

topics.label: AS 5 (2.4)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees accepted the company's own extraordinary-item classification uncritically, not testing it against AS 5's actual definition (an event clearly distinct from, and not part of, the ordinary business activity).

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: A construction contractor entered a fixed-price contract of ₹18,000 lacs to construct a bridge within 3 years, with provisions for variations. (₹ in lacs): Year 1/2/3 — Initial revenue agreed 18,000/18,000/18,000; Variation in revenue (+)400/400 (Years 2,3); Contract costs incurred to date 4,186/12,336*/16,200**; Estimated profit for whole contract 1,900/2,000/2,000. *includes ₹200 lacs standard materials stored at site for use in Year 3. **excludes ₹200 lacs standard material brought forward from Year 2. Year 2's variation was approved by the customer. Compute year-wise: revenue recognised, expenses recognised, contract costs to complete, and profit/loss recognised.

Year 2: revenue 18,400, less profit 2,000 = total cost 16,400; cost incurred (excluding the ₹200 lacs stored materials not yet used) 12,336−200=12,136; degree of completion = 12,136/16,400 = 74%. Year 3: revenue 18,400, total cost 16,400; cost incurred 16,200+200 (bringing forward the previously-excluded stored material, now used) = 16,400; degree of completion 100%.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Class Ltd., a real-estate developer, purchased land for ₹225 crore in FY2025 intending a residential complex, then sold it a few months later for ₹360 crore due to a strategic reallocation and favourable market conditions. All legal formalities completed. Advise on revenue recognition for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html:
AS 9 recognises revenue when earned with reasonable certainty of collection, arising from the enterprise's ordinary activities. Class Ltd. is in the business of buying and selling properties; the land forms part of its inventory. The ₹360 crore sale is therefore a transaction arising from ordinary activities, and revenue is recognised when the sale is completed and collection is reasonably certain.

Per AS 5, this is not an extraordinary item, since it arises in the ordinary course of business — though given its size, its nature and amount should be separately disclosed if relevant to explaining the enterprise's performance. The ₹360 crore is recognised as revenue in the year the sale is completed.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees treated the large, unusual sale as an extraordinary item given its size and the company's stated change in strategy, missing that dealing in land is Class Ltd.'s core ordinary business, so scale alone does not make a transaction extraordinary.

question_html: Machinery purchased 1st April, 2020 for ₹10 lakhs, useful life 5 years, residual value (at 2020 prices) ₹10 lakhs. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025 per AS 10 (Revised).

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Zenith Ltd. constructed a machine for its own use, total cost ₹5,00,000, completed 1st April, 2024, useful life 10 years; the company did not commence using the machine until 31st March, 2025. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html: ₹50,000 (₹5,00,000/10 years). Depreciation begins from the date the machine is ready for use (1st April, 2024), regardless of when actual use commenced — the fact that it sat idle for a period after being ready is not relevant to when depreciation begins.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees charged no depreciation at all, reasoning the machine was never actually used during the year, missing that "ready for use" (not actual use) triggers depreciation.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Another machine was purchased 1st April, 2022, for ₹50,000, useful life 5 years, nil residual value. On 1st April, 2024, management decided the machine would now be used for only two more years. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html: Original SLM depreciation = ₹50,000/5 = ₹10,000/year. Net book value on 1st April, 2024 (after 2 years) = 50,000−20,000 = ₹30,000. With the revised remaining useful life of 2 years, the unamortised cost is spread over the revised remaining life: 30,000/2 = ₹15,000/year for the next 2 years.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees continued the original ₹10,000/year rate, not recognising that a revised useful-life estimate requires recomputing the annual charge over the remaining life going forward.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Mediwell Hospitals Ltd. acquired 40 Doppler Scan Machines from Holiver Inc., USA, at US$1,65,100/unit at the start of FY2022-23, exchange rate ₹50/US$. Partly financed by a government grant of ₹5 crores (specific condition: refund on change in management/ownership control). In April 2025, 51% shareholding acquired by an overseas investor — management control changed, grant refund now due. Useful life 5 years, SLM at 20% p.a. Also: Bank charges US$4,000 (whole import), Sea freight ₹7,500/unit. No Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account was maintained for the grant. Advise the accounting treatment for the grant refund per AS 12.
answer_html:
The grant was received towards a fixed asset; the capital (deduction-from-cost) approach was adopted (confirmed by the absence of a Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account).

Cost of asset (1,65,100 × 40 units × ₹50)3,302 lakhs
Add: Freight and other charges (4,000×50 bank charges + 7,500×40 sea freight)5 lakhs
Total cost3,307 lakhs
Less: Grant received(500 lakhs)
Cost as per AS 10 (net of grant)2,807 lakhs
Less: Depreciation for 3 years (2,807 × 20% × 3)(1,684.2 lakhs)
Carrying amount as on 1.4.2025 (before refund)1,122.8 lakhs
Add: Grant refunded500 lakhs
Revised carrying amount1,622.8 lakhs

Per AS 12, when a grant that was deducted from an asset's cost becomes refundable, the amount refundable is added back to the carrying amount of the asset (or the gross book value increased), rather than expensed — increasing the future depreciation charge over the asset's remaining life.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees expensed the refunded grant amount directly to the P&L, not applying AS 12's specific rule that a refund of a grant deducted from asset cost is added back to the carrying amount of that asset.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Mr. Rohan acquired 200 equity shares of Zeta Technologies Ltd. on a cum-right basis for ₹1,40,000 as a long-term investment. The company announced a 1:1 rights issue at ₹214/share. Mr. Rohan did not subscribe, instead selling his rights entitlement for ₹24,000. After the shares became ex-rights, the market value of his existing 200 shares fell to ₹1,20,000. State the appropriate accounting treatment for the sale of rights and the fall in market value, per AS 13.
answer_html:
Per AS 13, when investments are acquired cum-right and the market value immediately after becoming ex-rights is lower than cost, it may be appropriate to apply the rights sale proceeds to reduce the carrying amount of the investment to its (ex-rights) market value.

Here, cost ₹1,40,000; ex-rights market value ₹1,20,000 — a decline of ₹20,000. Of the ₹24,000 rights sale proceeds, ₹20,000 is applied to reduce the carrying amount from ₹1,40,000 to ₹1,20,000 (its ex-rights market value); the balance ₹4,000 (24,000−20,000) is credited to the Profit and Loss Account as income.

The investment in the 200 equity shares is shown at a carrying amount of ₹1,20,000 in Mr. Rohan's books.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees credited the entire ₹24,000 rights sale proceeds to P&L as income, not applying AS 13's rule that the portion covering the decline to ex-rights market value should instead reduce the investment's carrying amount.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Can interest be included in the cost of inventories?
answer_html:
As a general rule, AS 2 (para 12) provides that interest and other borrowing costs are usually not related to bringing inventories to their present location and condition, and are therefore usually excluded from inventory cost.

However, AS 16 (para 6) requires borrowing costs directly attributable to acquisition/construction/production of a qualifying asset to be capitalised, and para 5 specifically includes "inventories that require a substantial period of time to bring them to a saleable condition" as an example of a qualifying asset (e.g. liquor requiring 12+ months of maturation, per ASI 1). It is only in such exceptional cases — where time is a major factor in changing the condition of the inventory — that borrowing costs are included in inventory valuation. Routinely/repetitively manufactured inventory over a short period is never a qualifying asset, so its borrowing costs are never capitalised.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees answered with a flat "no", missing the exceptional qualifying-asset case (e.g. maturing liquor) where AS 16 does require capitalisation into inventory cost.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Garnet Limited has 4 operating segments (₹ in appropriate units): Fan — Inter-segment sales 3,200, External sales 10,900, Total assets 23,700; Light — 200, 1,400, 13,200; Lamp — 0, 1,500, 4,200; Printer — 1,100, 200, 3,400; Total — 4,500, 14,000, 44,500. How many reportable segments does Garnet Limited have per the Revenue and Assets criteria in AS 17? State reasons.
answer_html:
A segment is reportable if its revenue (external + inter-segment) is ≥10% of total revenue (external + internal, all segments), OR its assets are ≥10% of total assets.

Total revenue basis (external 14,000 + internal 4,500 = 18,500): 10% threshold = 1,850. Fan's total revenue (3,200+10,900=14,100) far exceeds 1,850 — Fan is reportable. (Light: 200+1,400=1,600, below threshold; Lamp: 0+1,500=1,500, below; Printer: 1,100+200=1,300, below.)

Assets basis (total 44,500): 10% threshold = 4,450. Fan (23,700) and Light (13,200) both exceed this — both are reportable on the assets criterion.

75% external-revenue test: reportable segments' external revenue must cover ≥75% of total external revenue (75% × 14,000 = 10,500). Fan and Light's combined external revenue (10,900+1,400=12,300) already exceeds 10,500, so no additional segments need to be added to meet the 75% threshold.

Conclusion: Garnet Limited has 2 reportable segments — Fan and Light (Fan qualifies on both revenue and assets; Light qualifies on assets only, but that alone is sufficient).

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees tested the 10% revenue threshold against external sales alone, omitting inter-segment sales from the revenue base used for that specific test.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Mr. Rajiv, a KMP of Raijada Limited, received a cheque of ₹70,000 towards reimbursement of expenses incurred on hotel stay, conference expenses, etc. while attending a meeting on behalf of the company. Is this transaction covered under AS-18?
answer_html: Mr. Rajiv, as a KMP, is a related party of Raijada Limited under AS 18. However, a reimbursement of expenses actually incurred on the company's behalf is not in the nature of remuneration or a related-party transaction requiring disclosure — it is simply the company bearing its own cost, routed through the KMP. Hence, this reimbursement need not be disclosed as a related-party transaction under AS 18.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees concluded disclosure was required simply because Mr. Rajiv is a related party, without separately testing whether the specific transaction (a cost reimbursement, not remuneration) actually falls within AS 18's disclosure scope.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 1st April, 2024, Mansi Ltd. sold a plant for ₹8,52,800 (carrying amount ₹1,80,000) as part of a sale-and-leaseback package with Akash Ltd., leasing the asset back for an 8-year term. Economic life of the asset is 8 years. Minimum lease rents ₹1,60,000/year, payable annually from 31st March, 2025. Mansi Ltd.'s incremental borrowing rate is 10% p.a. Calculate the net effect on the Statement of Profit and Loss in Mansi Ltd.'s (the lessee's) books.
answer_html:
Lease classification: lease term (8 years) covers the entire economic life (8 years). PV of minimum lease payments = ₹1,60,000 × 5.335 (annuity factor @10% for 8 years) = ₹8,53,600, which substantially covers the fair value/sale price (₹8,52,800). This is therefore a finance lease.

Per AS 19 para 48, where a sale-and-leaseback results in a finance lease, the profit on sale (₹8,52,800−₹1,80,000 = ₹6,72,800) is not recognised immediately — it is deferred and amortised over the lease term in proportion to the depreciation of the leased asset.

Assuming straight-line depreciation: Depreciation = ₹8,52,800/8 = ₹1,06,600/year. Deferred profit amortised = ₹6,72,800/8 = ₹84,100/year. Net effect on Statement of P&L = ₹1,06,600 − ₹84,100 = ₹22,500 debit per annum, for each of the 8 years of the lease term.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees recognised the full sale profit immediately in the year of sale, not applying AS 19's specific deferral-and-amortisation rule for a sale-and-leaseback that results in a finance lease.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Should appropriation to mandatory reserves be excluded from net profit attributable to equity shareholders? AB Limited must, per an agreement with debenture holders, appropriate profits each year to a specific reserve such that, at redemption, the reserve equals at least half the debenture value. Since these appropriations aren't available for distribution to equity shareholders, AB Limited excluded them from the Basic EPS numerator. Is this correct?
answer_html:
The appropriation to such a mandatory reserve should be included in net profit attributable to equity shareholders for computing Basic EPS — AB Limited's treatment is not correct.

AS 20 para 11 defines the numerator as net profit/loss for the period "attributable to equity shareholders" — after deducting preference dividends and attributable tax, but nothing else. Emphasis on "attributable to equity shareholders" (not "available for distribution") means amounts appropriated to mandatory reserves, though not distributable as dividend, remain attributable to equity shareholders in substance (the reserve still belongs to them, merely earmarked). They should therefore be included in the Basic EPS computation.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees conflated "attributable to equity shareholders" with "distributable to equity shareholders," incorrectly excluding non-distributable mandatory-reserve appropriations from the EPS numerator.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Swift Limited acquired patent rights to manufacture Solar Roof Top Panels for ₹600 lacs. Product life cycle estimated at 5 years; amortization decided in the ratio of future cash flows: Year 1–5: 300, 300, 300, 150, 150 (₹ lacs). After Year 3, estimated balance future life revised to 3 years, with expected cash flow after Year 5 of ₹75 lacs. Determine the amortization cost of the patent for each year per AS 26.
answer_html:
Years 1–3, amortized in the ratio of the originally estimated future cash flows 300:300:300:150:150 (total 1,200): each of Years 1, 2, 3 = ₹600 × 300/1,200 = ₹150 lacs/year.

Unamortized patent cost after Year 3 = 600−450 = ₹150 lacs, now amortized over the revised remaining life of 3 years (Years 4, 5, 6) in the ratio of the revised estimated future cash flows: 150:150:75 (i.e. 2:2:1). Year 4 = 150×2/5=₹60 lacs; Year 5 = ₹60 lacs; Year 6 = 150×1/5=₹30 lacs.

Total amortized over the patent's full (revised) life: 150+150+150+60+60+30 = ₹600 lacs, fully recovering the original cost.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees continued amortizing the remaining balance using the original 5-year cash-flow ratio, not re-basing the calculation on the revised 3-year remaining life and its own revised cash-flow estimates.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Briefly explain the scope and forms of Joint Venture as per AS 27.
answer_html:
Scope: AS 27 applies to accounting for interests in joint ventures and reporting joint venture assets, liabilities, income, and expenses in the financial statements of venturers and investors, regardless of the structure/form under which the joint venture activities take place. Its consolidated-financial-statements provisions apply only when the venturer prepares and presents CFS.

Forms of Joint Venture: (i) Jointly controlled operations — no separate entity created; venturers use their own resources, raise their own funds, incur expenses, and realise sales individually, using shared assets/employees alongside their own business, with no separate books maintained for the joint venture. (ii) Jointly controlled assets — no separate legal entity, but the venturers jointly own assets used to generate economic benefit for each of them, taking up related expenses/liabilities per the contractual agreement. (iii) Jointly controlled entities — a new entity is created, pooling the venturers' resources; the entity purchases its own assets, incurs its own liabilities/expenses, and makes its own sales; the net result is shared per the contractual agreement, which also determines joint control; a separate set of books is maintained.

topics.title: Financial Reporting of Interests in Joint Ventures
topics.label: AS 27 (1.2)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees conflated jointly controlled assets with jointly controlled entities, missing that the defining distinction is the absence vs. presence of a separate legal entity and separate books.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: X Ltd. purchased a fixed asset four years ago for ₹150 lakhs, depreciating at 10% p.a. SLM. At the end of the fourth year, it revalued the asset to ₹75 lakhs, writing off the revaluation loss to P&L. On the revaluation date, market price is ₹67.50 lakhs, expected disposal costs ₹3 lakhs, and value in use is estimated at ₹60 lakhs. What is the treatment of impairment loss, given fair value for revaluation is market-value-based?
answer_html:
W.N. — Carrying amount at revaluation: Purchase price 150.00, less depreciation for 4 years (150/10 × 4) 60.00 = carrying value before revaluation 90.00, less downward revaluation charged to P&L (90−75) 15.00 = revalued carrying amount 75.00 lakhs.

Recoverable amount = higher of net selling price and value in use. Net selling price = market price 67.50 − disposal costs 3.00 = 64.50 lakhs. Value in use = 60 lakhs. Recoverable amount = ₹64.50 lakhs (the higher of the two).

Impairment loss = carrying amount (75.00) − recoverable amount (64.50) = ₹10.50 lakhs, recognised as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss immediately (since the prior downward revaluation was already charged to P&L rather than to a revaluation reserve, there is no reserve balance to absorb this further impairment against).

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees used the market price directly as net selling price without deducting disposal costs, or used net selling price as recoverable amount without comparing it against value in use to find the higher of the two.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: An oil company has been contaminating land for several years, not cleaning up since no legislation currently requires it. At 31st March, 2025, it is virtually certain that a law requiring clean-up of contaminated land will be enacted shortly after the year end. Is provisioning presently necessary?
answer_html:
Per AS 29 para 29, a past event creates a present obligation only when the enterprise has no realistic alternative to settling it. Environmental contamination alone does not create an obligation to remedy it unless a law requires the existing damage to be rectified — and where a proposed law's details are not yet finalised, an obligation arises only once enactment is virtually certain.

Here, it is virtually certain that a clean-up law will be enacted. The oil company must therefore provide for the clean-up cost in the year in which the legislation's enactment becomes virtually certain (the year ended 31st March, 2025) — not deferred until the law is actually enacted.

topics.title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topics.label: AS 29 (2.5)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees concluded no provision was needed since the law had not yet been enacted at the balance sheet date, missing that "virtually certain" enactment is itself sufficient to trigger the obligation under AS 29.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Write a short note on International Accounting Standard Board (IASB).
answer_html:
With a view of achieving the objective of setting global standards, the London based group namely the International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC), responsible for developing International Accounting Standards (IAS), was established in June, 1973.

  • It is presently known as International Accounting Standards Board (IASB).
  • Between 1973 and 2001, the IASC released IASs. Between 1997 and 1999, the IASC restructured their organisation, which resulted in formation of IASB. These changes came into effect on 1st April, 2001. Subsequently, IASB issued statements about current and future standards.
  • IASB publishes its Standards in a series of pronouncements called International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).
  • The standards issued by IASC till 31.03.2001 are known as IASs and the standards issued by IASB since 01.04.2001 are known as IFRSs.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees conflated the IASC and IASB timelines, or reversed which body issued IASs versus IFRSs, resulting in imprecise historical sequencing in their responses.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Giant Ltd. has entered into a binding agreement with Tiny Ltd. to buy a custom-made machine of ₹1,00,000 at the end of 2024-25, before delivery of the machine, Giant Ltd. had to change its method of production. The new method will not require the machine ordered and it will be scrapped after delivery. The expected scrap value is nil.

You are required to advise the accounting treatment and give necessary journal entry in the year 2024-25.
answer_html:
A liability is recognized when outflow of economic resources in settlement of a present obligation can be anticipated and the value of outflow can be reliably measured.

When flow of economic benefit to the enterprise beyond the current accounting period is considered improbable, the expenditure incurred is recognised as an expense rather than as an asset.

In the given case, Giant Ltd. should recognise a liability of ₹1,00,000 to Tiny Ltd.

Also, the flow of future economic benefit from the machine to the enterprise is improbable.

Thus, the entire amount of purchase price of the machine should be recognised as an expense.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Virat Traders, an unlisted partnership firm, had a turnover of ₹249.99 crore and borrowings of ₹25.01 crore during the financial year 2023-24. It is not a bank, financial institution, or insurance company, and also not a subsidiary of any other entity. The firm wishes to avail MSME exemptions for FY 2024-25. Is it eligible?
answer_html:
Company qualifies as an MSME if following conditions are satisfied:

  1. whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India;
  2. which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company;
  3. whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed 250 crore rupees in the immediately preceding accounting year;
  4. which does not have borrowings in excess of 50 crore rupees at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and
  5. which is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity which is not a MSME entity.

Yes, Virat Traders qualifies as an MSME since it meets all five criteria.

Further, it has been assumed that Virat Traders is not newly qualifying as an MSME in FY 2024-25 because a non-company entity that newly qualifies as an MSME can avail exemptions only after it remains as MSME for two consecutive years.

Until then, full AS compliance is required.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees applied the five MSME tests mechanically and concluded eligibility without addressing the two-consecutive-year assumption for newly-qualifying entities, missing part of what the question was testing.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: While preparing its financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2025, B Limited has come across the following events which took place after 31st March, 2025. The financial statements of the company were approved by the Board of Directors on 30th May, 2025: B Limited started negotiations with S Limited during 2024-25 to acquire their Consumer Durables Business for ₹400 lakhs. The deal was finalized on 20th April, 2025 and B Limited invested ₹275 lakhs before 30th May, 2025. You are required to state with reasons, whether the aforesaid event is an adjusting or non-adjusting event as per the provisions of the relevant AS.
answer_html:
AS 4 (Revised) defines “Events Occurring after the Balance Sheet Date” as those significant events, both favourable and unfavourable, that occur between the balance sheet date and the date on which the financial statements are approved by the Approving Authority in the case of a company.

The acquisition of Consumer Durables Business of S Limited by B Limited is an event occurring after the balance sheet date. However, it is a non-adjusting event as it does not affect the determination and the condition of the amounts stated in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2025. The disclosure should be made in the report of the approving authority about the investment of ₹275 lakhs to enable the users of financial statements to make proper evaluations and decisions.

question_html: Whether interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should be included in the segment expense or not?
answer_html: The interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should not be included as a part of the segment expense unless the operations of the segment are primarily of a financial nature or unless the interest is included as a part of the cost of inventories.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees included all interest expense indiscriminately in segment expense, overlooking the two exceptions (segment primarily financial in nature, or interest forming part of inventory cost) under which such interest is included.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Explain, in brief, the accounting treatment for an asset given under Operating Lease in the books of the Lessor.
answer_html:
The accounting treatment for an asset given under Operating Lease in the books of the lessor is given as under:

  1. The Lessor should present an asset given under Operating Lease as PPE in its balance sheet.
  2. Lease income from operating leases should be recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss on a straight-line basis over the lease term, unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern in which benefit derived from the use of the leased asset is diminished.
  3. Depreciation should be recognized in the books of the lessor. The depreciation of leased assets should be on a basis consistent with the normal accounting policy of the lessor for similar assets, and the depreciation charge should be calculated on the basis set out in AS 10.
  4. The impairment loss on assets given on operating leases are determined and treated as per AS 28.

examiner_comment.text: Many examinees conflated lessor and lessee treatments, describing finance-lease-style derecognition of the asset instead of the lessor retaining the asset as PPE and depreciating it under AS 10, resulting in partial credit loss.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of Passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the Passenger car segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner.

(i) You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a ‘Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.

(ii) If the company passes a resolution to sell some of the assets in the passenger car division and also to transfer few other assets of the passenger car division to the new factory, does this trigger the application of AS 24?

(iii) Would your answer to the above be different if the company resolves to sell the assets of the Passenger Car Division in a phased but time bound manner?
answer_html:
Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under para 3 of AS 24, ‘Discontinuing Operations'.

Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include: (1) Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service; (2) Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business; (3) Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and (4) Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

In view of the above the answers are:

(i) No, the companies' strategic plan has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Above all, the new segment i.e. commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.

(ii) No, the resolution is salient about stoppage of the Car segment in definite time period. Though, sale of some assets and some transfer proposal were passed through a resolution to the new factory, closure road map and new segment starting roadmap are missing. Hence, AS 24 will not be applicable.

(iii) Yes, phased and time bound programme resolved in the board clearly indicates the closure of the passenger car segment in a definite time frame and will constitute a clear roadmap. Hence, this action will attract compliance of AS 24.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees answered part (iii) without properly building on the reasoning already established in parts (i) and (ii), missing that a phased-but-time-bound board resolution is precisely the missing ingredient (a definite closure roadmap) that parts (i) and (ii) found absent, and so overlooked the requirement for a clear sale plan with time-bound actions when applying AS 24.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: A publisher owns 150 magazine titles of which 70 were purchased and 80 were self-created. The price paid for a purchased magazine title is recognised as an intangible asset. The costs of creating magazine titles and maintaining the existing titles are recognised as an expense when incurred. Cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each magazine title. Titles are managed by customer segments. The level of advertising income for a magazine title depends on the range of titles in the customer segment to which the magazine title relates. Management has a policy to abandon old titles before the end of their economic lives and replace them immediately with new titles for the same customer segment. Whether it will be a cash-generating unit as per AS 28?
answer_html: It is likely that the recoverable amount of an individual magazine title can be assessed. Even though the level of advertising income for a title is influenced, to a certain extent, by the other titles in the customer segment, cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each title. In addition, although titles are managed by customer segments, decisions to abandon titles are made on an individual title basis. Therefore, it is likely that individual magazine titles generate cash inflows that are largely independent one from another and that each magazine title is a separate cash-generating unit.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees identified the customer segment as the cash-generating unit because titles are managed and reported at that level, without recognising that CGU identification turns on independence of cash inflows, not on the level at which management happens to monitor performance.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Galaxy Limited is in the process of finalization of its accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2025 and needs your advice on the following issue in line with the provisions of AS 29: Galaxy Limited is selling cosmetic products under its brand name “Angel” but is getting these products manufactured from X Limited. It has an understanding (enforceable agreement) with X Limited that if the company becomes liable for any damage claims, due to any injury or harm to the customer of the cosmetic products, 40% shall be reimbursed to it by X Limited. During the year 2024-25, an estimate of the claim of ₹25 lakhs may be payable to the customers by Galaxy Limited. How should Galaxy Limited account for the claim that becomes payable?
answer_html: Since the understanding results in an enforceable agreement, the reimbursement of ₹10,00,000 (40% of ₹25,00,000) shall be recognized as a reimbursement right and provision will be recognized for the full amount of the liability of ₹25,00,000. The reimbursement right shall be treated as a separate asset and shall not be offset with the provision. In the Statement of Profit and Loss, the expense may be presented as ₹15,00,000 after offsetting the reimbursement right.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Galaxy Limited has been sued by one of its competitor for alleged infringement of trademark and a notice for levy of penalty of ₹50 lakhs has been received by it. The company has appointed a law firm to defend its case for a fee of ₹5 lakhs. 60% of the fees has been paid in advance and the rest 40% would be paid after finalization of the case. There are 70% chances that the penalty may not be imposed.
answer_html: As per AS 29, an obligation is a present obligation if, based on the evidence available, its existence at the balance sheet date is considered probable, i.e. more likely than not. Liability is a present obligation of the enterprise arising from the past events, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow from the enterprise of resources embodying economic benefits. In the given case, there are 70% chances that the penalty may not be levied. Accordingly, Galaxy Limited should not make the provision for liability. The matter is disclosed as a contingent liability unless the probability of any outflow is considered as remote. However, a provision should be made for the remaining 40% fees of the law firm amounting to ₹2,00,000 in the financial statements for 2024-25.

topics.title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topics.label: AS 29 (2.9)

examiner_comment.text: Several examinees recognised a provision for the trademark-suit penalty itself, treating a 30% chance of levy as sufficient to be "probable," when AS 29 requires the outflow to be more likely than not before a provision (rather than mere contingent-liability disclosure) is warranted; many also missed the separate, unconditional obligation to provide for the remaining unpaid law-firm fee.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html:
In G Ltd.'s books, closing inventory at 31.03.2024 was ₹10,40,000 (FIFO method). The company changes to weighted average method for 31.3.2024: closing inventory becomes ₹8,80,000. Realisable value at 31.03.2024 is ₹12,00,000. What will be the value of inventory in the books and what disclosure should be given?

  1. The value will be ₹8,80,000 and the fact that the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
  2. The value will be ₹12,00,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
  3. The value will be ₹12,00,000, and the fact that the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
  4. The value will be ₹8,80,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
answer_html: Answer: (iv) — inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value; the weighted-average cost (₹8,80,000) is lower than NRV (₹12,00,000), so ₹8,80,000 is the book value. Since this is a change in accounting policy (costing formula) with a material effect, AS 1/AS 2 require full disclosure, including the quantified amount of the effect of the change (not merely the fact of the change).

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees selected the "fact only" disclosure option instead of the "full disclosure with amount" option, understating the disclosure actually required for a material accounting policy change.

extraction_note: Question/options verbatim; source gives only "(iv)". Relevant to the AS 2 chapter book.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html:
Cost of a current investment acquired was ₹1000 but fair value was ₹800; recorded at ₹800. Now fair value of the investment is ₹1200. At what value should it be recorded, and how much gain credited to profit and loss?

  1. No change required; continues at ₹800.
  2. Recorded at ₹1000 and gain of ₹200 credited to P&L.
  3. Recorded at ₹1200 and gain of ₹400 credited to P&L.
  4. Recorded at ₹1200 but no gain credited to P&L.
answer_html: Answer: (ii) — current investments are carried at the lower of cost and fair value; even though fair value has now risen to ₹1,200 (above cost), the investment cannot be marked up beyond its original cost of ₹1,000. The carrying value is restored from ₹800 to ₹1,000 (the ceiling), recognising a gain of ₹200 (1,000−800) — the further rise from 1,000 to 1,200 is unrealised and not recognised.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees recorded the investment at the full current fair value of ₹1,200, not applying the cost ceiling that governs current-investment valuation under AS 13.

extraction_note: Question/options verbatim; source gives only "(ii)"; reasoning independently reproduces option (ii) exactly.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: As per the revised scheme effective from accounting periods commencing on or after 1st April, 2024, classify non-company entities for the purpose of applicability of Accounting Standards. Briefly explain the criteria for each category.
answer_html:
Non-company entities are classified into two categories: Micro, Small and Medium Sized Entities (MSMEs) and Large entities.

A non-company entity qualifies as an MSME if it satisfies all of: (i) its equity/debt securities are not listed or in the process of listing on any stock exchange (in India or abroad); (ii) it is not a bank, financial institution, or insurance company; (iii) turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed ₹250 crore in the immediately preceding accounting year; (iv) it does not have borrowings exceeding ₹50 crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and (v) it is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity that is not itself an MSME. These conditions are assessed as at the end of the relevant accounting period. A Large entity is any non-company entity that does not meet the MSME definition, and must comply in full with all Accounting Standards; MSMEs receive certain exemptions/relaxations.

examiner_comment.text: A direct recall question from the announcement text; common gaps include omitting one of the five MSME conditions, especially the holding/subsidiary condition.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Lion Ltd. (manufacturing/construction contracts), FY ended 31st March 2025, follows historical cost, FIFO, and percentage-of-completion. During the year, management changes: (i) inventory valuation FIFO→Weighted Average (citing raw-material price volatility); (ii) depreciation SLM→WDV (citing better usage reflection). The company discloses the inventory-method change in notes but not the depreciation-method change (calling it immaterial), and has not disclosed its accounting policy on government grants despite receiving a significant subsidy this year. (a) Identify AS 1 violations, if any. (b) Critically evaluate whether "materiality" justifies non-disclosure of a change in accounting policy. (c) Is the FIFO→Weighted Average change an estimate or policy change under AS 1?
answer_html:
(a) AS 1 requires all significant accounting policies to be disclosed, and any material change in policy to be disclosed along with its nature and reasons (with the effect indicated if ascertainable). Applying this: (1) Inventory method change (FIFO→Weighted Average) is a change in accounting policy, correctly disclosed with justification — compliant, provided the quantified effect is also disclosed or noted as unascertainable. (2) Depreciation method change (SLM→WDV) is technically a change in accounting estimate under AS 10, but AS 1 still requires disclosure of material items affecting the financial statements — depreciation affects profit, asset values, and return ratios; non-disclosure on unsubstantiated "immateriality" grounds is not appropriate without clear quantitative evidence. (3) Government grants policy non-disclosure: AS 1 requires disclosure of all significant accounting policies, including for government grants received — non-disclosure here is a violation of AS 1.

(b) Materiality is assessed by an item's potential to influence users' economic decisions. A depreciation-method change affects profit, asset values, and tax, and even a quantitatively modest impact may carry qualitative significance for comparability/trend analysis. The company's blanket reliance on "materiality" to justify non-disclosure is not valid unless supported by concrete evidence that the impact is immaterial both quantitatively and qualitatively.

(c) The change from FIFO to Weighted Average is a change in accounting policy (not a change in accounting estimate) — it is a change in the cost formula used to measure inventory, and its nature and financial impact should be properly disclosed.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees classified the depreciation-method change purely as an "estimate change" and concluded no AS 1 disclosure duty arose at all, missing that AS 1's materiality-based disclosure requirement applies regardless of whether the underlying item is technically a policy or an estimate change.

extraction_note: Verbatim from CAInter-AdvAcc-RTP-Sep2025-Q.pdf, full working shown in source. Kept as one connected record (three sub-questions all testing AS 1 disclosure principles against the same company's facts), not split, consistent with the precedent set for similarly-structured questions in other sittings.

Fixed overhead ₹95,000, including ₹15,000 godown rent (for storing finished products, not a production cost). 1,000 units of by-product BY also emerged, sold @₹12/unit after ₹2,500 expense; ₹4,800 realized from scrap sale. Average market price: FP1 ₹160/unit, FP2 ₹100/unit. Calculate the value of closing stock per AS 2.
answer_html:
Per AS 2, most by-products/scrap are measured at NRV, deducted from the cost of the main product.

NRV of by-product BY: Selling price (1,000×₹12) 12,000, less separate processing charges 2,500 = ₹9,500.

Joint cost to allocate: Raw material 3,20,000 + Labour 1,60,000 + Direct expenses 78,000 + Fixed overhead (95,000−15,000 godown rent, excluded as unrelated to production) 80,000 = 6,38,000; less NRV of BY (9,500) and scrap sale value (4,800) = ₹6,23,700 to allocate between FP1 and FP2.

FP1FP2
Output (units)3,0001,600
Sales price/unit₹160₹100
Sales value4,80,0001,60,000
Allocation ratio31
Joint cost allocated (3:1)4,67,7751,55,925

Since both FP1 (₹155.93 cost vs ₹160 selling price) and FP2 (₹97.45 vs ₹100) sell above cost, both finished goods are valued at cost, and the raw material feeding them is valued at its own cost (₹35/unit, not written down to the ₹20 replacement cost).

Closing inventory: FP1 (500×₹155.93) = ₹77,965. FP2 (300×₹97.45) = ₹29,235. Raw material (700×₹35) = ₹24,500. Total closing inventory = ₹77,965 + ₹29,235 + ₹24,500 = ₹1,31,700.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees included the godown rent (storage cost unrelated to production, per AS 2's general exclusion of storage costs) in the joint cost pool, or wrote raw material down to replacement cost despite both finished goods selling above their allocated cost.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Kiran Ltd. Balance Sheets (2024/2025): Share capital 12,00,000/12,00,000; P&L A/c 8,50,000/10,00,000; Long Term Loans 10,00,000/10,60,000; Trade payables 3,50,000/4,00,000; Fixed Assets 17,00,000/20,00,000; Investment in shares 2,00,000/2,00,000; Inventory 6,80,000/7,00,000; Trade receivables 7,20,000/6,60,000; Cash 60,000/70,000; Bills Receivable 40,000/30,000. Income Statement 2025: Sales 40,80,000; Cost of sales 27,20,000; Gross Profit 13,60,000; Admin expenses 4,60,000; Depreciation 2,20,000; Operating Profit 6,80,000; Dividend received 50,000; Interest paid 1,40,000; PBT 5,90,000; Tax 2,60,000; PAT 3,30,000. Retained earnings: Opening 8,50,000 + Profit 3,30,000 − Dividend paid 1,80,000 = Closing 10,00,000. Prepare the Cash Flow Statement using the indirect method.
answer_html:
(i) Cash flows from operating activities: PBT 5,90,000 + Depreciation 2,20,000 + Interest (non-operating) 1,40,000 = 9,50,000; less Dividend received (non-operating) (50,000) = Operating Profit before WC changes 9,00,000; add Decrease in Bills Receivable 10,000, Decrease in Trade receivables 60,000, Increase in Trade payables 50,000 = 10,20,000; less Increase in inventory (20,000) = Cash flow from operations before tax 10,00,000; less Tax paid (2,60,000) = Cash flow from operating activities: ₹7,40,000.

(ii) Cash flows from investing activities: Purchase of fixed assets (20,00,000+2,20,000 depreciation−17,00,000 opening = 5,20,000) outflow (5,20,000); Dividend on investments received 50,000 = Cash used in investing activities: ₹(4,70,000).

(iii) Cash flows from financing activities: Long term loan taken 60,000; Interest paid (1,40,000); Dividend paid (1,80,000) = Cash used in financing activities: ₹(2,60,000).

Net increase in cash: ₹10,000 (7,40,000−4,70,000−2,60,000). Opening cash 60,000 + 10,000 = Closing cash balance ₹70,000 (matches given).

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Garden Ltd. acquired plant and machinery for ₹20 lakhs and sold furniture and fixtures for ₹5 lakhs in the same year. Can the company disclose net cash outflow towards purchase of fixed assets in the cash flow statement per AS 3?
answer_html: No. Per AS 3 para 21, major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments from investing and financing activities must be reported separately, except for the specific items permitted to be reported net under paras 22 and 24 — acquisition and disposal of fixed assets is not among those permitted items. The company cannot net the ₹20 lakh purchase against the ₹5 lakh disposal; both must be shown as separate gross cash flow lines.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees assumed netting was acceptable since both items relate to fixed assets, not checking the specific, limited list of items AS 3 actually permits to be reported net.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: When can an item qualify to be a prior period item as per AS 5?
answer_html: Per AS 5 para 16, prior period items are income or expenses that arise in the current period as a result of errors or omissions in the preparation of financial statements of one or more prior periods. The term does not include other adjustments necessitated by circumstances that, though related to prior periods, are determined only in the current period (e.g. arrears payable to workers from a retrospective wage revision).

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: A Ltd. finds that the stock sheets of 31.3.2024 did not include two pages containing details of inventory worth ₹20 lakhs. How should this be dealt with in the accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2025, per AS 5?
answer_html: This omission is a prior period item under AS 5 para 16. Per para 19, prior period items are normally included in determining the current period's net profit or loss — so ₹20 lakhs should be added to the opening stock as at 1.4.2024. Alternatively, such items may be shown in the statement of profit and loss after the current period's net profit/loss has been determined. Either presentation must clearly indicate the effect of the item on the current period's profit or loss.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: A company took a construction contract for ₹100 lakhs in January 2024; 80% completed at cost ₹92 lakhs by 31.3.2025; further ₹23 lakhs estimated to complete; expected loss ₹15 lakhs. Can the company recognise the loss in the FY2024-25 financial statements?
answer_html: Yes. Per AS 7 paras 31 and 35, an expected loss on a construction contract must be recognised as an expense immediately, regardless of (i) whether work has commenced; (ii) the stage of completion; or (iii) profits expected on other contracts. The company must recognise the ₹15 lakh loss immediately in the year ended 31.3.2025.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees deferred the loss recognition to future periods or spread it across the remaining completion percentage, missing AS 7's requirement for immediate full recognition.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Tonk Tanners (leather shoes): On 31st December, 2024, shoes worth ₹3,20,000 were sent to Mohan Shoes for sale on consignment; 25% remained unsold with Mohan Shoes as on 31st March, 2025. Advise when revenue is recognised in 2024-25 per AS 9.
answer_html: Mohan Shoes is a consignee (agent), not a buyer — risk and reward remain with Tonk Tanners until Mohan Shoes sells to a third party. Revenue is recognised only for the goods actually sold by the consignee: ₹3,20,000 × 75% = ₹2,40,000 recognised as revenue in 2024-25; the remaining 25% (unsold) stays as Tonk Tanners' closing inventory.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 10th January, 2025, Tonk Tanners supplied shoes worth ₹4,50,000 to Shani Shoes and concurrently agreed to repurchase the same goods on 11th April, 2025. Advise on revenue recognition.
answer_html: A sale with a concurrent agreement to repurchase the same goods is, in substance, a financing arrangement, not a genuine sale. The resulting cash inflow is not revenue and should not be recognised as revenue in 2024-25.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees recognised the ₹4,50,000 as ordinary sales revenue, not recognising the repurchase commitment as converting the transaction into a financing arrangement in substance.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 21st March, 2025, shoes worth ₹1,60,000 were sold to Shoe Shine, but due to their showroom refurbishment, delivery was made on 12th April, 2025 at their request. Advise on revenue recognition.
answer_html: If, on 21st March 2025, Shoe Shine took title and accepted billing for the goods, the sale is complete and all risks/rewards of ownership have transferred, even though physical delivery was delayed at the buyer's own request. subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 1st December 2024, Precision Tools Ltd. replaced the motor of an old machine with a new one costing ₹1,20,000, improving output capacity by 15%. The old motor had cost ₹50,000 and accumulated depreciation ₹35,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized.
answer_html: Carrying amount of the old motor = 50,000−35,000 = ₹15,000, which is derecognised (written off) since it is being replaced. The new motor's acquisition cost of ₹1,20,000 is capitalised as a separate component (component accounting under AS 10). Net effect: ₹1,20,000 capitalised, ₹15,000 carrying amount of the old motor removed/expensed.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees simply added the new motor's cost to the machine's carrying value without also derecognising the replaced motor's remaining carrying amount.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 15th March 2025, Precision Tools Ltd. shifted a machine from one factory to another, incurring: Dismantling cost ₹12,000; Transport and installation ₹18,000; Loss due to damage in transit ₹6,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized.
answer_html: Nil is capitalised — costs of relocating or reorganising part or all of an enterprise's operations are not included in the carrying amount of PPE under AS 10. The entire ₹36,000 (12,000+18,000+6,000) is charged off to the Profit and Loss Account.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees capitalised the transport and installation cost, reasoning it was directly attributable to the machine, missing AS 10's specific exclusion of relocation costs regardless of their connection to a particular asset.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd. received ₹65 lakhs from a local authority to develop medical facilities for employees at its new township. Explain the accounting treatment per AS 12.
answer_html: This is a grant in the nature of a revenue grant (related to employee welfare expenditure, not a specific fixed asset). Such grants are generally presented as a credit in the Statement of Profit and Loss, either separately or under "Other Income." Alternatively, the ₹65 lakhs may be deducted from the related expense (employee benefit expenses) instead.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees treated this as a capital grant since it funds facilities at a "newly built" site, missing that the grant's purpose (employee welfare) rather than the site's newness determines its revenue-grant classification.
