subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd. also received ₹82 lakhs as a Central Government subsidy for establishing a new production unit in a notified backward area, classified as being in the nature of promoters' contribution, intended to support long-term development. Explain the treatment per AS 12.
answer_html: Per AS 12, grants in the nature of promoters' contribution — given with reference to total investment/capital outlay, with no repayment ordinarily expected — are treated as Capital Reserve, which can neither be distributed as dividend nor treated as deferred income. Since this ₹82 lakh subsidy is neither tied to a specific fixed asset nor to revenue, the full amount should be credited to Capital Reserve.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees treated this as deferred income to be amortised, not recognising the promoters'-contribution characterisation that requires direct Capital Reserve treatment.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 1st April 2024, Kesar held 75,000 equity shares of Beta Ltd. at book value ₹15/share (nominal ₹10 each). Transactions: 20th June 2024, purchased 15,000 additional shares at ₹16/share. 1st August 2024, Beta Ltd. declared a 1:6 bonus issue. 31st October 2024, rights issue of 3-for-7 held at ₹15/share; Kesar sold one-third of his rights entitlement to Megha at ₹2/share and subscribed to the remainder on 5th November 2024. Prepare the Investment Account in Kesar's books for the year ending 31st March 2025.
answer_html:
W.N.1 Bonus shares: (75,000+15,000)/6 = 15,000 bonus shares (holding at bonus date: 90,000).

W.N.2 Rights entitlement: (75,000+15,000+15,000)/7 × 3 = 45,000 rights shares entitlement (on a holding of 1,05,000 post-bonus).

W.N.3 Sale of rights: One-third of 45,000 = 15,000 shares' worth of entitlement sold × ₹2/share = ₹30,000, credited to Statement of Profit and Loss (proceeds from renouncing rights, not adding to the investment's cost).

W.N.4 Rights subscribed: Remaining two-thirds of 45,000 = 30,000 shares subscribed × ₹15/share = ₹4,50,000.

Investment Account (Equity shares in Beta Ltd.): Dr: To Balance b/d 75,000 shares ₹11,25,000; To Bank A/c (20.6.24 purchase) 15,000 shares ₹2,40,000; To Bonus issue (W.N.1) 15,000 shares — Nil cost; To Bank A/c (rights subscribed, W.N.4) 30,000 shares ₹4,50,000. Total: 1,35,000 shares, ₹18,15,000. Cr: By Balance c/d (balancing figure) 1,35,000 shares ₹18,15,000.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees credited the full rights-sale proceeds to reduce the cost of the remaining investment instead of crediting them to profit and loss, or miscounted the bonus/rights entitlement base by using the wrong holding figure at each successive corporate action.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: X Co. Ltd. (share capital ₹50 lakhs, equity shares of ₹10 each) was taken over by Y Co. Ltd. X Co. Ltd. has General Reserve ₹10,00,000 and Profit and Loss account Cr. ₹5,00,000. Y Co. Journal entries (books of Y Co. Ltd.):

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Is it permissible to capitalise borrowing costs incurred on assets necessary for the construction of qualifying assets? A company constructing a large manufacturing plant in a backward area also purchased a residential building (funded by a long-term loan) to house workers engaged in the plant's construction, intending to dispose of the building once construction completes. If the manufacturing plant is a qualifying asset, are the borrowing costs on the residential-building loan eligible for capitalisation?
answer_html:
Per AS 16 para 3, a qualifying asset "necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale"; para 5 clarifies that assets ready for use when acquired are not qualifying assets. Prima facie, the residential building appears ready for use on acquisition, suggesting no capitalisation.

However, since providing housing is necessary for the construction of the plant, the borrowing costs on the building loan are, in substance, directly attributable to the construction of the manufacturing plant. The company should therefore capitalise these borrowing costs as part of the cost of the manufacturing plant, up to the period the plant is ready for its intended use.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees stopped at the observation that the residential building is itself "ready for use" and concluded no capitalisation applies, missing the substance-over-form link to the main construction project's necessity.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Cotton Garments Limited, 5 segments (₹ Crore): Segment Assets A/B/C/D/E 40/15/10/10/5 (Total 80); Segment Results (95)/5/5/(5)/15 (Total −75); Segment Revenue 310/40/30/40/30 (Total 450). The Chief Accountant believes only segment "A" should be reported. Examine this opinion per AS 17.
answer_html:
Per AS 17 para 27, a segment is reportable if: (i) its revenue (external+internal) is ≥10% of total revenue; or (ii) its result (profit or loss) is ≥10% of the combined result of all profit-making segments or all loss-making segments, whichever is greater in absolute amount; or (iii) its assets are ≥10% of total assets. If reportable segments cover <75% of total external revenue, additional segments must be added until 75% is reached.

(a) Revenue test (10% of 450 = 45): only A (310) qualifies.

(b) Result test: combined profit-segments (B+C+E = 5+5+15=25) vs. combined loss-segments (A+D = 95+5=100, in absolute terms); greater = 100; 10% = 10. Segments with |result| ≥10: A (95) and E (15) qualify.

(c) Assets test (10% of 80 = 8): A, B, C, D (40,15,10,10) qualify; only E (5) falls short.

Since every segment (A through E) satisfies at least one of the three tests, all five segments must be reported per AS 17. The Chief Accountant's opinion that only segment A is reportable is therefore wrong.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees checked only the revenue test (which favours only segment A) and stopped there, missing that the result and assets tests bring in the remaining segments too.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: X Ltd. sold goods to its associate company for the 1st quarter ending 30.6.2024, priced as it would for any ordinary customer. After that quarter, the related party relationship ceased to exist. Decide whether transactions for the entire year have to be disclosed as related party transactions.
answer_html: No. Per AS 18 para 23, only the transactions during the period the related party relationship actually existed — here, the first quarter ending 30.6.2024 — need be disclosed as related party transactions. Transactions in the remaining periods, after the relationship ceased, need not be disclosed as such.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 1st April, 2024, Mansi Ltd. sold a plant for ₹8,52,800 (carrying amount ₹1,80,000) as part of a sale-and-leaseback package with Akash Ltd., leasing the asset back for an 8-year term. Economic life 8 years. Minimum lease rents ₹1,60,000/year, payable annually from 31st March, 2025. Incremental borrowing rate 10% p.a. Calculate the net effect on the Statement of Profit and Loss in Mansi Ltd.'s (lessee's) books.
answer_html:
Lease classification: lease term (8 years) = entire economic life (8 years). PV of minimum lease payments = ₹1,60,000 × 5.335 (annuity factor @10% for 8 years) = ₹8,53,600, substantially covering the fair value/sale price (₹8,52,800). This is a finance lease.

Per AS 19 para 48, where a sale-and-leaseback results in a finance lease, the profit on sale (₹8,52,800−₹1,80,000 = ₹6,72,800) is not recognised immediately — deferred and amortised over the lease term in proportion to the leased asset's depreciation.

Assuming straight-line depreciation: Depreciation = ₹8,52,800/8 = ₹1,06,600/year. Amortised deferred profit = ₹6,72,800/8 = ₹84,100/year. Net effect on Statement of P&L = ₹1,06,600 − ₹84,100 = ₹22,500 debit per annum, for each of the 8 years of the lease term.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees recognised the full sale profit immediately in the year of sale, not applying AS 19's deferral-and-amortisation rule for a sale-and-leaseback resulting in a finance lease.
